the effects of fibre size and shape on the carcinogenicity, and hence toxicity, of asbestos.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
long, thin chrysotile fibres are the most carcinogenic.
the occurrence of cancer is associated most closely with exposure to long, thin asbestos fibres, and that this relationship is consistent with the results of animal studies and physical models.
the carcinogenic potency of asbestos is related to fibre length and diameter, with fibres 5-10 μm in length and 0.25 um in diameter being associated most strongly with increased lung cancer risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
lung cancer is associated with exposure to asbestos, and that the association is stronger for longer, thinner fibres.
lung cancer risk is increased by exposure to long thin chrysotile fibres and is associated with exposure to fibres throughout a range of length and diameters.
the carcinogenic potency of asbestos is related to the length and diameter of the fibres, with the most carcinogenic being long thin fibres (10–20 μm in length and <0.2 μm in width).
The main takeaway from our work is that
long thin asbestos fiberes, such as chrysotile, may be more carcinogenic than shorter thicker fibres.
the risk of lung cancer in asbestos workers is more strongly related to long thin fibrous particles than to other fibre dimensions, such as length alone, or diameter alone.
the relationship between fibre size and cancer risk is complex.
